Tour Eiffel.text: Gustave Eiffel's wrought-iron tower, built for the 1889 World's Fair and meant to stand twenty years. At 330 m it was the tallest structure in the world until 1930.

Arc de Triomphe.text: Commissioned by Napoleon after Austerlitz, it stands at the centre of the Étoile, where twelve avenues meet. The Unknown Soldier lies beneath it, under an eternal flame.

Palais du Louvre.text: A fortress, then the kings' palace, then the world's most visited museum. Its wings enclose the Cour Carrée and the Cour Napoléon.

Louvre Pyramid.text: I. M. Pei's glass and steel pyramid, 21 m high, made the Louvre's main entrance. Controversial when it opened, it is now one of the city's icons.

Notre-Dame.text: The Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, with its two towers, rose windows and flying buttresses. Restored after the 2019 fire and reopened in December 2024.

Sainte-Chapelle.text: Louis IX's palace chapel, built to hold the Crown of Thorns. Its upper chapel is walled almost entirely in fifteen-metre stained-glass windows.

Dôme des Invalides.text: Hardouin-Mansart's gilded dome over the Invalides, the soldiers' hospital of Louis XIV. Napoleon's tomb lies beneath it.

Musée d'Orsay.text: The Gare d'Orsay, a railway station built for the 1900 World's Fair, became the museum of Impressionist art. The great clocks still face the Seine.

Palais Garnier.text: Charles Garnier's opera house, the showpiece of Second Empire Paris, with its gilded groups, green dome and grand staircase.

Place de la Concorde.text: The largest square in Paris, where the guillotine stood during the Revolution. The Luxor Obelisk, over 3,000 years old, came from Egypt in 1833.

Grand Palais.text: Built for the 1900 World's Fair, with the largest glass roof in Europe over its nave. It hosts exhibitions, fairs and the 2024 Olympic fencing.

Petit Palais.text: Also built for the 1900 fair, facing the Grand Palais. Now the city's fine-arts museum, entered through a great gilded gate.

Place Vendôme.text: Hardouin-Mansart's octagonal square of uniform facades. The Vendôme Column, cast from cannon captured at Austerlitz, stands in the middle.

Colonne Vendôme.text: Napoleon's bronze column, modelled on Trajan's, its spiral frieze made from 1,250 captured cannon. Pulled down in 1871 by the Commune and rebuilt.

Église de la Madeleine.text: A Roman temple in Paris, with 52 Corinthian columns. Napoleon planned it as a temple to his army's glory; it became a church.

Assemblée nationale — portico.text: The Palais Bourbon, seat of the French National Assembly. Its twelve-column portico was added to face the Madeleine across the Concorde.

Institut de France.text: Le Vau's domed college facing the Louvre across the Pont des Arts. It is home to the Académie française and four other academies.

Palais de Chaillot.text: Built for the 1937 World's Fair, its two curved wings frame the most famous view of the Eiffel Tower, across the Seine.

Parvis du Trocadéro.text: The Parvis des Droits de l'Homme, between the wings of Chaillot, lined with gilded bronze statues. Everyone photographs the Eiffel Tower from here.

École Militaire.text: Gabriel's officers' school at the end of the Champ de Mars. Napoleon trained here in 1784–85.

Colonnes de Buren.text: Daniel Buren's 260 black-and-white striped columns in the Cour d'Honneur of the Palais-Royal. Controversial at first, now much loved.

Palais-Royal — galleries.text: Cardinal Richelieu's palace. Its arcaded galleries round a quiet garden were the busiest pleasure ground in Paris before the Revolution.

Hôtel de Ville.text: Paris's city hall, rebuilt in neo-Renaissance style after the Commune burned the old one in 1871.

Tour Saint-Jacques.text: The flamboyant Gothic bell tower of a church destroyed in the Revolution. Pascal is said to have experimented with air pressure here.

Centre Pompidou.text: Piano and Rogers's inside-out building: its pipes, ducts and escalators on the outside, colour-coded by use. Home to the national museum of modern art.

Colonne de Juillet.text: The July Column at the Place de la Bastille, where the fortress stood. It honours the dead of the 1830 revolution; the gilded Genius of Liberty tops it.

Place des Vosges.text: The oldest planned square in Paris: 36 brick and stone houses round a garden, the king's pavilion on one side and the queen's on the other.

Monument à la République.text: Marianne, the Republic, raising an olive branch, with Liberty, Equality and Fraternity at her feet and the lion of universal suffrage.

Cirque d'Hiver.text: Hittorff's polygonal winter circus, still a working circus, with its bronze horsemen and frieze of riders.

Opéra Bastille.text: Carlos Ott's modern opera house on the Place de la Bastille, opened for the bicentenary of the Revolution.

Hôtel de Sens.text: One of the few medieval town houses left in Paris, built for the archbishops of Sens, with its turrets and gothic gateway.

Église Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis.text: The Jesuits' church in the Marais, with one of the first domes in Paris.

Église Saint-Gervais.text: A Gothic church behind the Hôtel de Ville, with the first classical facade in Paris: three stacked orders of columns.

Pont Neuf.text: Despite its name, the oldest standing bridge in Paris. Twelve arches, half-moon bays over every pier, and 381 grotesque heads under its cornice.

Pont Alexandre III.text: A single steel arch over the Seine, named for the Tsar, with gilded winged horses on its four pylons. Many call it the most beautiful bridge in Paris.

Pont des Arts.text: An iron footbridge between the Louvre and the Institut, once famous for its love locks, which were removed in 2015.

Pont de Bir-Hakeim.text: A two-level bridge: cars and bikes below, Métro Line 6 above on an iron colonnade. Seen in 'Inception' and 'Last Tango in Paris'.

Fontaine des Innocents.text: The oldest monumental fountain in Paris, a Renaissance loggia by Jean Goujon, now in the square at Les Halles.

Fontaine Saint-Michel.text: Davioud's wall fountain at the Place Saint-Michel: the archangel slaying the devil, between red marble columns. A classic meeting point.

Flamme de la Liberté.text: A life-size copy of the Statue of Liberty's torch flame, given by the USA. Above the Alma tunnel, it became an informal memorial to Diana.

Louis XIV — Place des Victoires.text: Bosio's statue of Louis XIV on a rearing horse, balanced on its hind legs alone, in Hardouin-Mansart's circular square.

Foch — Place du Trocadéro.text: Marshal Foch, commander of the Allied armies in 1918, rides facing the Eiffel Tower across the Seine.

Rue de Rivoli — arcades.text: Napoleon's grand street along the Tuileries and the Louvre. Its uniform arcades shelter shops and cafés for a kilometre.

Sacré-Cœur.text: The white basilica on the top of Montmartre, the highest point in Paris.

Panthéon.text: A church turned into the resting place of the nation's great: Voltaire, Rousseau, Hugo, Curie.

Tour Montparnasse.text: Paris's only skyscraper in the centre. Its ugliness led to the 1977 ban on tall buildings in the city.
